key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: SUDDEN onset within 12-48 hours, often 30 minutes to 2 hours AFTER A FATTY MEAL (fried foods, heavy meals). LOCATION: Right upper quadrant (RUQ), precisely localized just below right rib cage. RADIATES TO RIGHT SHOULDER OR SCAPULA (phrenic nerve referred pain). DURATION: CONSTANT pain lasting >6 hours (unlike biliary colic <6 hours). CHARACTER: SHARP or ACHING, CONSTANT (NOT colicky). AGGRAVATING: WORSE WITH DEEP BREATHING, movement, and fatty food intake. Trigger is fatty meals. RELIEVING: NOTHING relieves pain effectively. Position changes don't help. Pain persists despite rest. TIMING: CONSTANT (not episodic like biliary colic). Lasts >6 hours continuously. SEVERITY: 7-10/10, severe and unrelenting. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: NAUSEA AND VOMITING very common, fever (100.5-102°F) within 12-24 hours, MURPHY'S SIGN (inspiratory arrest during right upper quadrant (RUQ) palpation), anorexia. May have jaundice if common bile duct involved. KEY POSITIVES: right upper quadrant (RUQ) tenderness, Murphy's sign, post-fatty meal onset, fever. KEY NEGATIVES: Diarrhea uncommon. Left-sided pain rules out. Pain resolving <1-2 hours suggests biliary colic not cholecystitis.

red_flags: High fever >102.5°F with rigors - suggests gangrenous cholecystitis or ascending cholangitis
Jaundice with confusion or sepsis - ascending cholangitis, needs urgent ERCP
Severe right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain with hypotension - gallbladder perforation or septic shock, call 911
Elderly or diabetic patients - higher risk of gangrenous cholecystitis and perforation
